title: Sharding and partitioning
scopeHtml:
Scope: range, hash, directory partitioning, shard key choice, cross-shard queries.

Scope: range, hash, directory partitioning, shard key choice, cross-shard queries.

notes.title: Why shard
notes.html:
Sharding (partitioning) splits one big dataset across many machines, each holding a slice. Replication copies the same data; sharding divides different data. You shard when data or write volume exceeds one machine.

Triggers (rough numbers): a single database over 2 to 5 TB, write rate beyond what one primary can fsync (around 10k to 50k simple writes/s depending on hardware), or working set no longer fitting in RAM.

Worked example. 6 TB of orders, 20,000 writes/s peak. One Postgres node tops out near 8,000 writes/s with that data size. 4 shards: 1.5 TB and 5,000 writes/s each, with headroom.

Decision gravity. Sharding is the biggest one-way door in data architecture: every query, join, transaction and migration changes. Exhaust cheaper steps first: indexes, caching, read replicas, bigger machine, archive old data. Instagram, Notion and Figma all sharded Postgres only after years of single-node growth.

Industry examples. Instagram sharded Postgres by user id with logical shards mapped to physical servers. Vitess shards MySQL for YouTube and Slack. MongoDB and Cassandra shard natively.

Everyday analogy. A library too big for one building: books A-H in building 1, I-P in building 2. Finding a book is easy if you know the rule, awful if you need all the books about "ships".

Common interview traps.

  • Sharding at 50 GB. Premature, and permanent.
  • Confusing sharding with replication, or saying you shard "for availability".

notes.title: Range partitioning
notes.html:
Each shard owns a continuous range of the key. Shard 1: A to F, shard 2: G to M, and so on. Or by date: January in one partition, February in the next.

Strengths: range scans are cheap (WHERE created_at BETWEEN ... touches one or two shards) and ordering is preserved. Weakness: hot spots. If keys are sequential (timestamps, auto-increment ids), all new writes go to the last range.

Shard A: user_id 0        .. 25,000,000
Shard B: user_id 25,000,001 .. 50,000,000
Shard C: user_id 50,000,001 .. 75,000,000   <- all new signups land here

Worked example. Time-series metrics partitioned by day: today's partition gets 100% of writes (say 50k/s) while 29 older partitions sit idle. Fix: prefix the key with a bucket (sensor_id then time) so writes spread over sensors, while a single sensor's range is still contiguous.

Industry examples. HBase and Bigtable use range-partitioned tablets that split automatically when they grow; Postgres declarative partitioning PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) is common for logs and archiving (drop an old partition instantly instead of a huge DELETE). Spanner and CockroachDB are range-based with automatic splits.

CREATE TABLE events (id bigint, created_at timestamptz, payload jsonb)
  PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
CREATE TABLE events_2026_11 PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-11-01') TO ('2026-12-01');

Decision gravity. Choose for range queries and time-based retention. Alternative: hash. Breaks with monotonic keys. Re-splitting ranges is reversible if the system splits automatically (Bigtable), painful if you hand-managed it.

Everyday analogy. A dictionary split into volumes A-C, D-F and so on: great for looking up all words starting "pre", but everyone writing new words for "Z" crowds one volume.

Common interview traps.

  • Range partitioning on timestamp for a write-heavy table.
  • Ignoring skew in the key (more surnames starting with S than Q).

notes.title: Hash partitioning
notes.html:
Compute hash(key) and map it to a shard. A good hash spreads keys evenly, so no hot range, but neighbouring keys end up on different shards, so range scans touch every shard.

Two ways to map hash to shard:

  • Modulo: shard = hash(key) % N. Dead simple, but changing N moves almost every key (going 4 to 5 shards relocates about 80% of data).
  • Consistent hashing / fixed slots: place shards and keys on a ring (or divide hash space into many fixed slots, for example Redis Cluster's 16,384 slots, and assign slots to nodes). Adding a node moves only about 1/N of the keys.

Worked example. 4 shards with modulo: key hash 17 goes to shard 1. Add a fifth shard: 17 % 5 = 2, so it moves. Of 100M keys, about 80M move, a night of heavy copying. With 16,384 slots, adding a node moves only the slots handed over (about 3,277 slots, 20%).

Virtual nodes. A physical node owns many ring positions (for example 256 vnodes) so load is smooth and a failed node's data spreads over many peers instead of doubling one neighbour. Cassandra defaults changed from 256 to a lower vnode count in newer versions (confirm in docs).

# Redis Cluster: slots 0-16383 divided among 3 masters
# node A: 0-5460, node B: 5461-10922, node C: 10923-16383
cluster-enabled: yes
cluster-node-timeout: 15000

Industry examples. DynamoDB and Cassandra (hash of partition key, ring), Redis Cluster (slots), MongoDB hashed shard keys, Memcached clients with consistent hashing.

Decision gravity. Chosen when access is mostly by key and load balance matters. Breaks for range queries and for one celebrity key (hash cannot split a single key). Choosing slots up front (many more than machines) keeps this reversible.

Everyday analogy. Dealing a deck of cards to players: everybody gets a fair mix, but you cannot hand out "all hearts in order" to one player.

Common interview traps.

  • hash % N with no plan for resizing.
  • Believing hashing fixes hot keys; one viral key still lands on one shard.

notes.title: Directory-based partitioning
notes.html:
A lookup table (the directory) says which shard owns each key or key group. Instead of a formula, you store the mapping: tenant 7 -> shard 3.

Strengths: total flexibility. You can move one big tenant alone, give VIP customers their own hardware, and rebalance without changing a hash function. Weakness: the directory is a critical dependency; it must be fast (cached), highly available and consistent.

Worked example. SaaS with 20,000 tenants. Mapping table has 20,000 rows (tiny, cached in each app server with 60 s TTL and invalidation on change). Tenant "BigCorp" uses 40% of the load, so it gets shard 9 alone; everyone else is spread over shards 1 to 8.

A common compromise is logical shards: hash the key into, say, 1,024 logical shards, and keep a small directory mapping logical shard to physical server. Moving one logical shard is a small, targeted copy. Instagram used this approach.

CREATE TABLE shard_map (
  tenant_id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  shard_id  int NOT NULL,
  state     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'  -- ACTIVE, MIGRATING
);

Industry examples. Vitess (VSchema and topology server), Slack's workspace-to-shard mapping, Salesforce multi-tenant orgs, Figma's and Notion's logical shard to physical database maps.

Decision gravity. Most flexible, so best for B2B multi-tenant data; the cost is an extra hop and a new service to keep alive. Reversible, as you can always change entries.

Everyday analogy. A hotel front desk keeping a list "guest X is in room 412" rather than assigning rooms by alphabet.

Common interview traps.

  • Making the directory a single point of failure or an uncached per-request lookup.
  • Forgetting to describe how the directory is updated safely during a migration.

notes.title: Choosing a shard key
notes.html:
The shard key is the column that decides where a row lives. It is the most important and least reversible choice.

A good key has:

  1. High cardinality (millions of distinct values, not 5 countries).
  2. Even distribution of load, not just of rows.
  3. Present in most queries, so each query hits one shard.
  4. Stable (changing it means moving the row).

Examples:

System Good key Bad key Why
Chat messages conversation_id message timestamp Timestamp is hot-tail
E-commerce orders customer_id order_status Status has 5 values, skewed
Multi-tenant SaaS tenant_id country A few huge countries
Social posts author_id (with care) post_id auto-increment Sequential hot shard

Worked example. Orders sharded by customer_id: "show my orders" hits 1 shard (5 ms). "All orders today for the CFO report" hits 16 shards, merges them: 80 ms and 16 times the load. That second query should go to a warehouse, not production shards.

Compound keys. Use (tenant_id, user_id) or add a random suffix (salting) for hot entities. Cassandra's partition key plus clustering key is exactly this: the partition key picks the node, clustering key orders rows inside.

Industry examples. Instagram: user id embedded in 64-bit ids (41 bits time, 13 bits shard id, 10 bits sequence), so any id tells you its shard. Twitter Snowflake ids are time-sortable. Uber's schemaless/Docstore shard by entity uuid.

Decision gravity. One-way door: resharding to a new key means rewriting all data and every query. Design the key from the top 3 queries, not from the table shape.

Everyday analogy. Sorting mail into pigeonholes by street name versus by "first letter of house colour"; the second rule is useless to the postman.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing a key that matches the schema but not the access pattern.
  • Low-cardinality keys (country, boolean flags).
  • Forgetting that unique constraints and foreign keys only work within a shard.

notes.title: Cross-shard queries, joins and transactions
notes.html:
Once data is split, anything that touches more than one shard gets harder and slower.

Options:

  • Scatter-gather: ask every shard, merge results. Latency = slowest shard (p99 of N shards is much worse than p99 of one). With 16 shards each having a 1% chance of a slow response, about 15% of requests hit at least one slow shard.
  • Denormalize / co-locate: keep related rows on the same shard (orders and order_items both sharded by customer_id). Joins stay local.
  • Global/reference tables: copy small, rarely changing tables (countries, currencies) to every shard.
  • Secondary index tables: a second table sharded by a different key (email to user_id), maintained asynchronously or transactionally.
  • Analytics elsewhere: stream changes to a warehouse (see warehouses note).

Cross-shard transactions.

  • Two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then commit. Correct but blocks if the coordinator dies, and is slow.
  • Saga: sequence of local transactions with compensating actions (refund if shipping fails). Eventually consistent, no locks.
  • Better: design so one business transaction stays inside one shard.
Pagination across shards: ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000
Each shard must return its top 1020, coordinator merges and discards.
Deep offsets cost shards x offset rows. Use keyset pagination (WHERE id < last_seen).

Worked example. Fan-out count query across 32 shards where each shard answers in 10 ms median, 200 ms p99: the fan-out call's median is closer to the per-shard p90, around 40 to 60 ms, and its p99 is dominated by the worst shard.

Industry examples. Vitess handles scatter queries and offers vindexes for secondary lookup; CockroachDB and Spanner do distributed transactions with consensus per range plus 2PC across ranges; Citus (Postgres) uses co-located distributed tables and reference tables; Elasticsearch scatter-gathers every query by design.

Decision gravity. Accept cross-shard queries only for rare admin or reporting paths. If core user flows need them, the shard key is wrong.

Everyday analogy. Counting everybody's savings across 16 banks: you must phone each bank and wait for the slowest one.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing 2PC casually; explain its blocking and latency costs.
  • Offset pagination across shards.
  • Assuming auto-increment ids, uniqueness and foreign keys work globally.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Shard only when one machine cannot hold the data or write rate; it is a one-way door.
  • Range: ordered, great for scans, hot-spots on sequential keys. Hash: even load, no scans; use many fixed slots or consistent hashing, not % N.
  • Directory: flexible mapping table (or logical to physical shards); must be cached and highly available.
  • Shard key: high cardinality, even load, in most queries, stable. Derive it from the top queries.
  • Cross-shard work is expensive: co-locate data, denormalize, reference tables, secondary indexes, sagas over 2PC, analytics in a warehouse.

questions.promptHtml: What is sharding, how does it differ from replication, and when do you actually shard?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you know sharding is a costly one-way door and not a first resort.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Replication copies the same data to several machines; sharding splits different data across machines, each owning a slice. I shard when data or write volume no longer fits one machine, for example a few TB, or writes beyond what one primary can fsync, or a working set bigger than RAM. Before that I exhaust cheaper steps: indexes, caching, read replicas, a bigger machine, archiving old data.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A router (app library, proxy, or the database itself) maps each key to the shard that owns it.

Client -> App -> Router -> Shard 1 (keys A)
                        -> Shard 2 (keys B)
                        -> Shard 3 (keys C)

Example: 6 TB of orders, 20,000 writes/s peak. One Postgres node tops out near 8,000 writes/s at that size. Four shards give 1.5 TB and about 5,000 writes/s each, with headroom.

What gets harder: joins across shards, transactions, unique constraints, secondary indexes, pagination, schema changes, backups, and every migration. That is why it is the biggest one-way door in data architecture. Instagram, Notion and Figma sharded Postgres only after years on a single node.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sharding at 50 GB.
  • Saying you shard for availability (that is replication).
  • Skipping the cheaper steps.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do you try first? -> Query/index tuning, cache, read replicas, vertical scale, archive cold data, functional split by service.
  2. Does each shard need replicas? -> Yes; sharding does not give availability.
  3. What breaks first in the app? -> Cross-shard joins and transactions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "shard when the DB is slow". The senior gives thresholds, lists cheaper alternatives, and names what is lost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A startup sharded a 200 GB database early and spent a year building cross-shard reports that a read replica would have served.

questions.promptHtml: Why is hash(key) % N a poor way to map keys to shards, and what do you use instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Resizing is the real test of a partitioning scheme.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With modulo, changing N remaps almost every key: going from 4 to 5 shards moves about 80% of the data. Instead I use many fixed slots (for example 16,384 in Redis Cluster) assigned to nodes, or a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes. Adding a node then moves only about 1/N of the keys.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Modulo: key hash 17 goes to shard 1 when N=4 (17 % 4) and shard 2 when N=5. Most keys change shard, so adding a node means a night of copying and cache misses.

Slots: slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384; a table maps slots to nodes. Adding a node hands over some slots (about 3,277 of 16,384, or 20%, for 4 to 5 nodes).

Ring with vnodes: nodes own many positions (for example 256) on the ring; a key goes to the next position clockwise. Load is smooth and a failed node's data spreads over many peers instead of doubling one neighbour.

# Redis Cluster: 3 masters share slots 0-16383
# node A: 0-5460, node B: 5461-10922, node C: 10923-16383
cluster-enabled: yes
cluster-node-timeout: 15000

Hash partitioning spreads load evenly but kills range scans, and one hot key still lands on one shard.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Modulo with no resize plan.
  • Believing hashing fixes hot keys.
  • Few slots (cannot spread to many nodes later).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How many slots/logical shards should I pre-create? -> Far more than machines, 1,024 to 4,096, so you can grow without remapping.
  2. Why vnodes? -> Even load and distributed recovery.
  3. How do range queries work on hash partitions? -> Scatter to all shards, or keep a secondary ordered index.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer knows the term "consistent hashing". The senior computes the moved-data fraction and prefers fixed logical shards with a map.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cache fleet resized with modulo; hit rate dropped to 20% for an hour and the database fell over.

questions.contextHtml: An IoT platform stores sensor readings in a range-partitioned store, key = timestamp, one partition per day. 50,000 inserts/s all day, 29 older partitions are only read occasionally. Dashboards: one partition node at 95% CPU and 8 ms write p99 on that node going to 400 ms; the other 29 nodes at 3% CPU. Total cluster looks "fine" at 12% average.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more nodes." New nodes would own old, idle days; today's partition stays on one node.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How are reads shaped (per sensor over a time range, or all sensors for a time)? Is the store able to split ranges automatically? How long is retention?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed or buffer non-critical writes (queue and batch), raise write batch size, scale the hot node vertically if possible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) monotonic key on a range partition: all writes go to the newest range (matches the numbers); b) a bad single sensor (check key distribution); c) disk/compaction on that node.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-partition write rate metric, top-N keys sample, compaction stats.
  5. Root cause: Sequential keys make the last range the only one accepting writes, so cluster capacity is irrelevant.
  6. Fix: Change the key to (sensor_id, timestamp) or (bucket = hash(sensor_id) % 64, timestamp) so writes spread across sensors while a sensor's readings remain contiguous. Keep time partitioning for retention (drop a day instantly).
  7. Prevention: Review rule: no monotonic key as the first column of a range key; load-test with production-shaped keys; alert on per-partition skew.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The new key makes "all sensors in the last minute" a scatter query; if that is a dashboard, add a rollup table. I would not salt blindly without checking read paths.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What about cross-sensor time range queries? -> 64 buckets means 64 parallel range reads; use a pre-aggregated table.
  • Can you fix without a migration? -> Not for the key itself; write new data in the new layout and backfill.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team used a UUID v1 (time-based) as a key in a range-partitioned store and re-created exactly this hotspot; UUID v4 fixed writes but ruined range scans.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds nodes.
  • Hire: spots monotonic key, proposes sensor-first compound key.
  • Strong hire: weighs read-path cost, keeps retention benefit, adds skew monitoring.

questions.contextHtml: A B2B SaaS has 20,000 tenants and 600M rows. The largest tenant has 12% of all rows; the top 10 have 35%. The main queries: (1) all records for a tenant (95% of traffic), (2) lookup a user by email at login (before the tenant is known), (3) a nightly admin report over all tenants. Candidate shard keys: tenant_id, country, record_id (auto-increment).
questions.promptHtml: Pick a shard key and handle the awkward queries.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks country (low cardinality, skew) or record_id (every tenant query scatters).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can a user belong to several tenants? How big can one tenant grow? Are there cross-tenant features? Compliance on data location?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) tenant_id with a directory (logical shards): serves 95% of traffic from one shard; b) hash of tenant_id: no directory but whales cannot be isolated; c) record_id: every query scatters.
  4. How I'd verify each: Simulate shard load using real tenant sizes; compute the largest shard share.
  5. Root cause of difficulty: Skewed tenants and a query (login by email) that does not carry the shard key.
  6. Fix: Shard by tenant_id into 1,024 logical shards, mapped by a small cached directory to physical servers; give the 12% tenant its own server. Login: a global lookup table email -> tenant_id (small, replicated everywhere or its own sharded table by email), updated transactionally or via outbox. Nightly report: stream changes to a warehouse and run it there.
  7. Prevention: Per-shard size and QPS dashboard, rule that every query includes tenant_id, tests for queries that scatter.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The secondary lookup table can lag, so a just-registered user may not log in for a second; acceptable with a retry. I would not use country and I would not run the report on production shards.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A tenant outgrows one shard? -> Sub-shard by (tenant_id, user_id) for that tenant, a directory entry per sub-range.
  • Tenant wants data in EU only? -> Directory maps tenant to a region-pinned shard.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team chose tenant_id % N; a whale tenant doubled and its shard ran hot for months because there was no way to move one tenant.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: low-cardinality or sequential key.
  • Hire: tenant_id with a plan for login and reports.
  • Strong hire: logical shards plus directory, whale isolation, global lookup table consistency.

questions.contextHtml:
A session cache layer uses client-side sharding over 4 Redis nodes. Next week traffic doubles, and a teammate's change to 5 nodes goes to production at noon. Code:

int shardFor(String key, int nodes) {
    return Math.abs(key.hashCode()) % nodes;
}
Redis pick(String key) { return pool.get(shardFor(key, pool.size())); }
fun shardFor(key: String, nodes: Int): Int = Math.abs(key.hashCode()) % nodes
fun pick(key: String): Redis = pool[shardFor(key, pool.size)]

After the change: cache hit ratio drops from 96% to 21%, DB CPU goes from 30% to 100%, users get logged out.
questions.promptHtml: List all bugs/risks in this design and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only mentions the DB load and says "warm the cache first".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are these sessions or a pure cache? Is the pool resized often? Are clients all running the same shard function?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back to 4 nodes (the old mapping returns instantly, entries are still there), or rate-limit cache-miss DB fallbacks to protect the DB.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) modulo remap: about 80% of keys move when N goes 4 to 5 (matches 96% to 21%); b) bug in Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) (stays negative, negative index, exception for that 1 in 4 billion key); c) mixed client versions.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute the new shard for a sample of 10k real keys and count changes; check client version metrics.
  5. Root cause: Modulo mapping ties every key's home to N, so resizing is a mass remap and a cache avalanche. Also Math.abs of a hash can be negative for MIN_VALUE.
  6. Fix: Short term: roll back, warm up gradually. Long term: consistent hashing with vnodes, or 16,384 fixed slots mapped to nodes (Redis Cluster does this). Use Math.floorMod.
  7. Prevention: Resizing runbook with a calculated moved fraction, canary one node, DB fallback with a circuit breaker.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Consistent hashing still remaps about 1/N keys; for sessions that matter, a persistent store beats a cache. I would not resize at peak noon.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• With a ring, how many keys move 4 to 5 nodes? -> About 20%.
  • Do you need a coordinator? -> Redis Cluster nodes gossip the slot map; client libraries cache it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A resize at lunch time logged out a million users; the fix took five minutes, the rollback of cache keys took an afternoon.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the DB.
  • Hire: identifies modulo remap and proposes consistent hashing/slots.
  • Strong hire: computes moved fraction, spots the abs bug, adds rollout safety.

questions.contextHtml:
An order-search endpoint fans out to 32 shards and merges. Per-shard latency: median 10 ms, p99 200 ms. After a feature launch, API p99 climbs from 90 ms to 650 ms and timeouts hit 3% of requests. Shard CPU is only 40%. A red herring: one shard shows a 5 minute compaction in its logs.

endpoint /orders/search   p50=48ms p95=210ms p99=650ms
fanout=32  timeout=500ms  retries=1
questions.promptHtml: Why is the endpoint slow when the shards look healthy, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Find the slow shard and fix it", ignoring that tail latency compounds with fan-out.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in the launch (new filter not on the shard key)? Is the fan-out sequential or parallel? Do retries amplify load?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Turn off retry for the search, reduce fan-out (restrict to a date or customer when provided), return partial results with a flag after 200 ms, cache popular searches.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) tail amplification: if each shard is slow 1% of the time, 1 - 0.99^32 is about 28% of requests hit at least one slow shard (matches p95 and p99 growth); b) retries doubling load on slow shards; c) one compacting shard (a contributor, not the cause); d) merge step cost.
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace per-shard timings for a sample, compute the fan-out percentile, check retry counts.
  5. Root cause: A query without the shard key forces scatter-gather, and latency equals the slowest shard, so p99 of the fan-out approximates the worst shard's tail.
  6. Fix: Short term: partial results, hedged requests (send a duplicate to a replica after the p95 time), no retries. Long term: a search index (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) fed by CDC for this query, or a secondary index table sharded by the filter field.
  7. Prevention: Query review that rejects non-shard-key queries on hot paths, fan-out dashboards, tail latency SLO per shard.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Hedging adds load (about 5% extra requests); a search index is eventually consistent. I would not add shards, which would increase fan-out and worsen the tail.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did median look fine? -> The median of the max of 32 draws is near the per-shard p98, but the endpoint median is dominated by many fast shards; the damage is in the tail.
  • What if the filter is rare? -> A global secondary index keyed by that field avoids fan-out.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "search by phone" feature fanned out to 64 shards; adding a phone-to-user lookup table removed 63 calls per request.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: hunts one slow shard.
  • Hire: explains tail amplification and removes the fan-out.
  • Strong hire: quantifies 1-0.99^32, uses hedging/partial results and a derived index, watches retry amplification.

questions.promptHtml: What is directory-based partitioning, what are logical shards, and what can go wrong with the directory?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most flexible scheme and the one most real systems end up with.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A directory is a lookup table that says which shard owns which key or tenant, instead of a formula. A common compromise is logical shards: hash the key into, say, 1,024 logical shards and keep a small table mapping each to a physical server, so moving data means moving one logical shard. The risks are the directory becoming a single point of failure or a per-request bottleneck, and updating it safely during a migration.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Benefits: move one big tenant alone, give a VIP its own hardware, rebalance without changing a hash function. Cost: an extra lookup and a new critical service.

CREATE TABLE shard_map (
  tenant_id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  shard_id  int NOT NULL,
  state     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'  -- ACTIVE, MIGRATING
);

Operating it: tiny (20,000 rows), cached in every app server with a 60 s TTL plus invalidation on change; backed by a replicated store (etcd, a replicated DB); app keeps working from cache if the directory is down. During a move, the state flips MIGRATING then ACTIVE, and the router blocks or dual-writes for the moving key only.

Instagram-style ids embed the shard id so an id alone tells you its shard.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Uncached per-request lookup.
  • Directory without HA.
  • No safe protocol to change a mapping (stale caches write to the old shard).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do stale caches cause bugs? -> A server with an old mapping writes to the old shard after the move; use versioned mappings and have the shard reject writes for keys it no longer owns.
  2. Directory vs hash? -> Hash needs no lookup but cannot isolate one tenant.
  3. Where is the directory stored? -> A small replicated, strongly consistent store (etcd/ZooKeeper or a database), cached at the edge.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "a lookup table". The senior designs caching, failure behaviour and the move protocol.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mapping service outage took down all writes because apps could not resolve shards; caching with stale-on-error fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: How do you handle a business operation that must change data on two shards? Compare 2PC and sagas.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether you can design around the problem rather than reach for distributed transactions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: First choice is to design the shard key so one business transaction stays on one shard. If not, 2PC is correct but blocks if the coordinator dies and is slow. A saga runs local transactions in sequence with compensating actions (refund if shipping fails): no locks, eventually consistent, but you must handle intermediate states and idempotency.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
2PC: coordinator sends prepare to all participants; each durably promises to commit and holds locks; on all yes the coordinator sends commit. If the coordinator crashes after prepare, participants hold locks until it recovers. Latency is two round trips plus fsyncs, and throughput drops under contention.

Saga: T1 (debit on shard A), T2 (credit on shard B); if T2 fails run C1 (refund A). Each step must be idempotent and retriable; use an outbox for reliable messaging.

Saga: ReserveStock(shard 3) -> ChargeCard(shard 7) -> CreateShipment(shard 9)
Fail at ChargeCard -> compensate: ReleaseStock

Systems like Spanner and CockroachDB do 2PC across ranges but with consensus-replicated participants, so coordinator failure is survivable.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Proposing 2PC casually.
  • Sagas without idempotency or a visible "pending" state.
  • Forgetting that unique constraints and foreign keys do not span shards.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if a compensation fails? -> Retry with backoff, then alert and park for manual handling.
  2. How does a user see a half-done saga? -> Explicit states like PENDING, shown in the UI.
  3. When is 2PC acceptable? -> Rare, low-contention, low-volume operations or inside a system that makes the coordinator fault tolerant.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer names the two patterns. The senior first removes the need via co-location, and designs states, idempotency and compensation failure paths.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-rolled 2PC left locked rows for 40 minutes after a coordinator crash.

questions.contextHtml:
An admin screen lists orders across 16 shards with ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET :off. Staff paging deep (OFFSET 50,000) trigger alerts: coordinator memory 6 GB, shard CPU spikes, request takes 14 s. The query planner is not the problem.

Per shard receives: ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50020
16 shards x 50,020 rows = 800,320 rows to the coordinator, 20 returned
questions.promptHtml: Why is it so costly and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an index on created_at." The index helps each shard sort, but the 800k rows still travel.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do users need random page jumps or just next/previous? Is it an admin-only path? Must it be real-time?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap the offset (for example 1,000), and rate-limit the endpoint.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) offset pagination across shards forces each shard to return offset+limit rows (matches); b) missing index (secondary); c) coordinator merge in memory.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-shard EXPLAIN ANALYZE, row counts returned, coordinator heap profile.
  5. Root cause: To find global rank 50,000 you cannot skip rows on any shard independently; each must return its top 50,020.
  6. Fix: Keyset pagination: the client sends the last seen (created_at, id); each shard runs WHERE (created_at, id) < (:ts, :id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 and the coordinator merges 16 x 20 = 320 rows. For arbitrary search, use a search index fed by CDC.
  7. Prevention: Lint/review rule against OFFSET on sharded tables, max page depth, load test with deep pages.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Keyset pagination loses "jump to page 2,500"; I would offer filters instead. I would not raise memory limits.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ties on created_at? -> Add a unique tiebreaker (id) to the sort key.
  • Total count? -> Approximate counts or a maintained counter table.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A support tool paging to page 900 brought down a reporting shard pool; keyset pagination cut it from 14 s to 80 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: index only.
  • Hire: explains offset+limit per shard and uses keyset.
  • Strong hire: gives the multi-shard merge cost, tie-breaking and an alternative for search.

questions.contextHtml: A founder says: "We hit 400 GB in Postgres and growth is 8% a month. Our CTO says we must shard now to be web-scale." Facts: 1 primary (16 vCPU, 64 GB RAM), 2 replicas, peak 1,800 writes/s, 9,000 reads/s, p99 query 40 ms, CPU averages 35%, the biggest table has 230 GB and a bloated index, and no query has been tuned in a year.
questions.promptHtml: What do you say about sharding now, and what is your plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Either "yes, shard now" (premature) or "no" without numbers or a trigger.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the working set size vs RAM? What is the SLO and what is the next 12 month forecast? Is the growth mostly old data? What is the disk and IOPS headroom?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A. I would project: 400 GB at 8%/month is about 1 TB in 12 months, 2.5 TB in 24 months.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (options): a) do not shard yet: tune, partition by time, archive, move to a bigger instance; b) functional split (move a heavy feature to its own database); c) shard now.
  4. How I'd verify each: Look at pg_stat_statements, cache hit ratio, index bloat, table size by age; run a capacity forecast.
  5. Root cause of the pressure: It is not yet a capacity problem: CPU 35%, writes at about 20% of a single node's ceiling, with obvious tuning left.
  6. Fix (plan): Now: reindex/bloat cleanup, time-partition the 230 GB table with retention or archive to cold storage, tune queries, add PgBouncer. In 6 months: re-measure. Prepare for sharding without doing it: carry a tenant or user id on every table, avoid cross-entity joins on new code, design ids to embed a shard id. Trigger: disk above 60% of the largest practical instance, or writes above 50% of the benchmarked ceiling.
  7. Prevention: Capacity dashboard with forecast and a written trigger.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sharding now costs a team-year and makes every feature slower to ship; it is a one-way door. I would not shard at 400 GB with 35% CPU. The preparation steps are cheap and reversible.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if growth jumps to 25% a month? -> Move the trigger earlier and start the logical-shard design.
  • Would Aurora/Citus/Vitess change the plan? -> They reduce the cost of sharding but still change query patterns; evaluate before building your own.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A company deferred sharding for two years by partitioning and archiving, then sharded in a planned quarter instead of an outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: agrees to shard or refuses without data.
  • Hire: shows numbers, cheaper steps and a trigger.
  • Strong hire: prepares for sharding (shard-key-ready schema), forecasts and names the one-way door.

questions.contextHtml:
After sharding users and orders by user_id across 8 PostgreSQL shards, these defects appear in the first week: duplicate emails across accounts, a foreign key error when creating an order for a user on another shard, and two different orders with id = 1042. The schema was copied to every shard unchanged:

CREATE TABLE users  (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, email text UNIQUE, ...);
CREATE TABLE orders (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
                     user_id bigint REFERENCES users(id), ...);

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add the constraint back with a global index", which is not available in plain sharded Postgres.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which table do orders join to, and are order ids exposed to clients? Is email lookup needed at login?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop sign-ups from creating duplicates via a unique email -> user_id mapping table in one place; block new orders for cross-shard users until fixed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) uniqueness is only per shard (matches); b) bigserial per shard restarts at 1 and collides; c) FK works within one database only, and users on another shard are invisible.
  4. How I'd verify each: Query each shard for duplicate emails, compare id ranges, check which shard the failing insert targeted.
  5. Root cause: Constraints, sequences and foreign keys are per database, so they stop at the shard boundary.
  6. Fix: Global ids: embed shard id (Instagram: 41 bits time, 13 bits shard, 10 bits sequence) or Snowflake-style ids; a global email -> user_id table sharded by email; drop cross-shard FKs and enforce in the app, co-locating orders with their user (shard by user_id, which already holds for orders).
  7. Prevention: Schema review checklist for sharded tables: no global unique constraints, ids generated by a service, no cross-shard FK.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The email table adds a hop and a consistency issue; use a transaction at signup or a reservation row. I would not rely on application-level "check then insert" without a unique reservation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not UUID v4? -> Works, but 16 bytes and poor index locality; time-sortable ids are friendlier.
  • Can I still join users and orders? -> Yes on the same shard, when sharded by user_id.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Two shards both created user id 5001 and a support tool merged their histories; the cleanup took weeks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot explain why constraints break.
  • Hire: names per-shard scope, proposes global ids and a lookup table.
  • Strong hire: co-locates data, gives id bit layout and reservation pattern.

questions.contextHtml: Tenant "BigCorp" generates 40% of load on shard 3 (p99 write 180 ms, CPU 92%). You use a directory (tenant_id -> shard_id) cached in 60 app servers (60 s TTL). You must move BigCorp (900 GB, 4,000 writes/s) to a new dedicated shard 9 with no downtime and no lost writes.
questions.promptHtml: Describe the migration, including the directory flip and how you handle stale caches.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Copy the data and update the directory", which loses writes made during the copy and lets stale caches write to the old shard.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a few seconds of write pause acceptable for BigCorp? Do reads need to be fresh? Is CDC available on shard 3?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Throttle BigCorp background jobs to relieve shard 3 during the move.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (approaches): a) snapshot, CDC catch-up, verify, brief write freeze, flip; b) app dual writes; c) downtime window.
  4. How I'd verify each: Row counts and checksums, shadow reads, CDC lag under 1 s before the flip.
  5. Root cause: N/A. The risks are in-flight writes and stale caches.
  6. Fix (steps): Set directory state MIGRATING (version 12). Backfill throttled (900 GB at 40 MB/s is about 6.3 hours) from a consistent snapshot, with CDC streaming changes since the snapshot. Verify with checksums. Freeze writes for BigCorp (3 s) in the router and on shard 3 (reject by trigger or role), wait for CDC lag 0, flip directory to shard 9 version 13, unfreeze. Shard 3 rejects writes for tenant 7 after the freeze, so a stale cache hitting it gets an error and refreshes the directory. Keep reverse replication 9 to 3 for days, then delete old rows.
  7. Prevention: Rehearse on a copy, directory entries carry version numbers, alert on rejected writes after flip.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not do app-level dual writes (partial failure) and I would not rely on cache TTL expiry alone, because 60 s of stale writes would go to the old shard.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cutover fails verification? -> Abort before the flip; the old shard is still the owner, so it is cheap to roll back.
  • A bug is found two days later? -> Reverse replication allows flipping back.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration relied on a 60 s cache TTL; 300 writes went to the old shard after cutover and had to be replayed from the binlog.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: copy then flip, no catch-up.
  • Hire: backfill plus CDC, verify, short freeze.
  • Strong hire: versioned directory, old shard rejects writes, reverse replication, rehearsal.
